title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 31
paragraphs: After Solon had moved Croesus to ask further with his story about Tellus—recounting how many marks of happiness the man possessed—the king asked again whom he had judged worthy to be placed next after him, supposing that he himself would certainly win at least the second place. But Solon replied: “Cleobis and Biton. These men, Argives by birth, had wealth enough to live on and, in addition, bodily strength such as I shall describe. Both had equally won prizes in the games, and the following tale is also told of them. There was a festival of Hera among the Argives, and it was absolutely necessary that their mother should be carried in a cart to the temple. But the oxen were not brought up from the field in time. Barred by the shortage of time from any other solution, the young men put themselves under the yoke and drew the wagon, their mother riding upon it. So they pulled it for forty-five stades and arrived at the temple. After they had accomplished this and had been seen by the gathered crowd, a most excellent ending was given to their lives, and in this matter the deity showed that it is better for a man to die than to continue living. For the Argive men stood around praising the strength of the young men, and the Argive women praised the mother for having been lucky enough to bear such sons. The mother, overjoyed both by the deed itself and by the reports of it, took her stand before the image of the goddess and prayed that she would grant to her sons Cleobis and Biton, who had so greatly honored her, the gift that is best for a man to receive. After this prayer, once the young men had sacrificed and feasted, they lay down to sleep inside the temple itself and never rose again, but were held fast in that final ending. The Argives had statues made in their likeness and dedicated them as offerings at Delphi, believing that they had proved themselves most excellent men.”
